newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Baker presents secret ideas on Western Sahara.
newsitem.headline: Baker presents secret ideas on Western Sahara.

text.p: Talks between Morocco and its Western Sahara foes, the Polisario Front, broke off suddenly on Tuesday after U.N. envoy James Baker presented new proposals to break the deadlock over the future of the former Spanish colony.
The talks, the first between opponents who fought a 16-year war over the mineral reach territory to be held in the presence of the U.N., had been due to run for three days and end on Wednesday.

But Baker, a former U.S. secretary of state, said that the two sides needed to return home to consult with political leaders after he had put forward some "bridging proposals" aimed at ending a dispute that has been rumbling since 1976 when the Spanish abandoned the territory.
Baker declined to give any details of the proposals, saying that one prior condition for the talks, held in an old fortress just outside Lisbon, was that they should be kept secret.

He had been asked by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan to weigh up whether a six-year-old settlement plan for the region, part of a ceasefire that has been in force since 1991, was still viable or whether a new approach was needed.

The plan calls for a referendum to be held in the territory but Rabat and the Algeria-backed Polisario cannot agree on who should be allowed to vote in the territory, fourth-fifths of which is under Moroccan control.
Baker said that the proposals were partially based on the existing plan but also contained new elements.

However, he added that he was now more optimistic about the propects for a peaceful resolution to the dispute after the two days of discussions. "I was pleasantly surprised by the tone and the spirit was excellent," he said.
If the response from Morocco and the Polisario, which wants to set up an independent state, was positive to the proposals, then a new round of direct talks could be convened as early as mid-July.
"I hope to hear very soon," he said.

The negotiations were attended by Moroccan Prime Minister Abdellatif Filali and the premier of the self-proclaimed Arab Sahara Democratic Republic (RASD), Mahfud El Beiba. Algeria and Mauritania also sent representatives.

Spain initially ceded the 250,000 square km (100,00 sq mile) territory to the joint control of Morocco and Mauritania, but the latter soon renounced its claims to the mostly desert territory with its potassium mines and rich Atlantic fishing grounds.

The U.N. has become increasingly frustrated at the failure to stage the referendum, initially set for January 1992. But at the same time, it fears the destabilising effect for the region of any renewed hostilities.
